lead: Moist air ties humidification, cooling towers and drying together, and this unit follows that single thread. You learn to read the psychrometric chart, to size a cooling tower from an enthalpy driving force, and to predict how long a wet solid takes to dry. After the unit you can set up the mass and enthalpy balances behind an air washer, a cooling tower and a rotary dryer.
about: The unit follows moist air from definitions to equipment. Chapter 7.1 defines humidity, relative humidity, dew point, humid heat and enthalpy; 7.2 puts these on the psychrometric chart and shows how to read and mix states; 7.3 adds the adiabatic saturation and wet-bulb lines that make the chart usable. Chapter 7.4 applies those lines to humidification and dehumidification, and 7.5 uses the same air–water contact to cool water in a cooling tower. The unit then turns to drying: 7.6 covers moisture equilibria, 7.7 the drying rate curve and drying time, 7.8 batch and continuous dryers with through-circulation, and 7.9 the design of dryers including rotary dryers.

chapters.idea: Every property of moist air follows from two numbers, the dry-bulb temperature and the amount of water vapour, and the rest are defined quantities you can compute.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter alone, so keep it short. Define absolute humidity (humidity ratio) Y as kg of water vapour per kg of dry air, with Y = 0.622 p_A/(P − p_A), where p_A is the partial pressure of vapour in kPa and P the total pressure. Define saturation humidity Y_s, relative humidity as 100 p_A/p_AS, and percentage humidity (percentage saturation) as 100 Y/Y_s at the same temperature; the two are close but not equal. Dew point is the temperature at which p_A equals the saturation pressure. Define humid volume (m³ per kg dry air), humid heat c_s = 1.005 + 1.88Y in kJ/(kg dry air·K) and enthalpy H = c_s(T − T_ref) + Y λ_ref, with λ_ref ≈ 2500 kJ/kg at 0 °C. Add vapour–liquid equilibrium and steam-table enthalpy of pure water, which the syllabi list.

figure.title: From two measured numbers to air properties
figure.aria: A five-step chain from dry-bulb temperature and relative humidity through vapour pressure and humidity to humid volume, humid heat and enthalpy.

chapters.example: Air at 40 °C and 20 % relative humidity flows at 101.3 kPa; the saturation pressure of water at 40 °C is 7.38 kPa. Find (a) the partial pressure of water vapour, (b) the absolute humidity, (c) the dew point, (d) the humid volume, (e) the humid heat and (f) the enthalpy above 0 °C. Answer: p_A = 0.20 × 7.38 = 1.48 kPa; Y = 0.622 × 1.48/(101.3 − 1.48) = 0.0092 kg/kg dry air; the dew point is the saturation temperature at 1.48 kPa, about 12.7 °C; humid volume = (1/28.97 + 0.0092/18.02) × 22.414 × (313.15/273.15) = 0.90 m³/kg dry air; c_s = 1.005 + 1.88 × 0.0092 = 1.022 kJ/(kg·K); H = 1.022 × 40 + 0.0092 × 2500 = 63.9 kJ/kg dry air.
chapters.trap: Treating relative humidity as the water content of the air: at the same Y, warm air has a lower RH. Also, percentage humidity and relative humidity are different numbers when the air is far from saturation.
chapters.prereq: School-level vapour pressure and the gas laws; no earlier unit needed.
chapters.leave: Chart reading to 7.2, wet-bulb temperature to 7.3, and all drying definitions to 7.6.

chapters.idea: The psychrometric chart draws all the humidity properties on one sheet so that two known values fix the state and everything else is read off.
chapters.depth: Also called the humidity chart or psychrometric chart. Axes: dry-bulb temperature on x, humidity Y on y. Show the saturation curve, the constant relative-humidity curves, dew point read along a horizontal line, adiabatic saturation and wet-bulb lines sloping down to the right, humid-volume lines and enthalpy lines near-parallel to the wet-bulb lines. State clearly that one chart is valid for one total pressure (1 atm) and for air–water only. Use it to fix a state from dry bulb plus wet bulb, or dry bulb plus dew point. Show the three paths: heating is horizontal, cooling is horizontal until the saturation curve and then along the curve, humidification runs up an adiabatic line. Show mixing of two streams by the lever rule: the mixture lies on the straight line joining the two states, nearer the larger mass flow.

figure.aria: Two air states plotted on dry-bulb and humidity axes with the mixture point lying on the straight line between them, closer to the larger stream.

chapters.example: Mix 100 kg dry air/h at 30 °C with Y = 0.010 and 50 kg dry air/h at 40 °C with Y = 0.020 at 1 atm. Find the mixture humidity and temperature. Humidity: Y = (100 × 0.010 + 50 × 0.020)/150 = 0.0133 kg/kg dry air. Enthalpies: h_A = 1.005 × 30 + 0.010 × (2500 + 1.88 × 30) = 55.7 kJ/kg; h_B = 1.005 × 40 + 0.020 × (2500 + 1.88 × 40) = 91.7 kJ/kg; h_mix = (100 × 55.7 + 50 × 91.7)/150 = 67.7 kJ/kg. Then 67.7 = 1.005T + 0.0133(2500 + 1.88T), so T = 33.4 °C, the same point the lever rule gives.
chapters.trap: Using the chart for a pressure other than the one it was drawn for, and reading enthalpy along a horizontal line instead of along a wet-bulb line.
chapters.prereq: 7.1 for the definitions plotted on the chart.
chapters.leave: The derivation of the wet-bulb line to 7.3 and air-conditioning equipment to 7.4.

chapters.idea: An adiabatic saturator and a wet-bulb thermometer both follow the same line of constant enthalpy, which is why wet-bulb temperature gives humidity.
chapters.depth: Take a stream of air over a water surface with no external heat: it cools and picks up vapour until it reaches the adiabatic saturation temperature T_as. Mass and enthalpy balance on the saturator give Y = Y_s(T_as) − (c_s/λ_s)(T − T_as), a straight line on the chart with slope −c_s/λ_s. Then treat the wet-bulb thermometer: sensible heat from the air to the wick equals latent heat carried away by evaporation, h_c(T − T_w) = k_Y λ (Y_s(T_w) − Y). The Lewis relation h_c/(k_Y c_s) ≈ 1 is what makes T_w equal T_as for air–water, and it does not hold for organic vapours. State the practical conditions: wick kept wet, air speed above about 3 m/s, radiation shielded. Show reading Y from dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperatures, and why wet bulb is the lower limit of adiabatic cooling.

figure.aria: A saturation curve and a straight adiabatic cooling line that meets it at the wet-bulb temperature of about 22 degrees Celsius.

chapters.example: Air at 40 °C dry bulb and 20 % relative humidity has Y = 0.0092 kg/kg dry air. It passes a wet-bulb thermometer and then an adiabatic saturator. Find the wet-bulb temperature and the humidity after the saturator. Try T_w = 22 °C: the saturation humidity is 0.0167 and c_s ≈ 1.04 kJ/(kg·K); the line gives Y = 0.0167 − (1.04/2450)(40 − 22) = 0.0091, matching the entering 0.0092, so T_w ≈ 22 °C. The air leaves the ideal saturator saturated at 22 °C with Y = 0.0167, so it gains 0.0075 kg of water per kg of dry air.
chapters.trap: Writing wet-bulb temperature equal to adiabatic saturation temperature for every vapour; they are equal only for air–water, where the Lewis relation holds.
chapters.prereq: 7.1 for humidity and enthalpy, 7.2 for reading the chart.
chapters.leave: Packed-tower design for humidifiers to 7.4 and the cooling-tower driving force to 7.5.

chapters.idea: Humidification and dehumidification are moves along chart paths, and the wet-bulb line sets the limit for humidifying air with recirculated water.
chapters.depth: Cover humidification methods: spray chamber or air washer, wetted-surface humidifier, steam injection. Cover dehumidification: cooling below the dew point with a coil, absorption with lithium chloride or glycol solutions, adsorption on silica gel, and compression. Work the paths on the chart for heating, cooling, humidifying, dehumidifying and mixing, which together are the air-conditioning processes. Treat the recirculating-water gas humidification system: water at the adiabatic saturation temperature, air moving along a wet-bulb line, so adiabatic humidification stops at saturation. Add a short design calculation for a packed humidifier using NTU and the enthalpy driving force, the same tool as in gas absorption. Keep it qualitative where the syllabi only say 'methods'.

figure.title: Air washer with recirculated water
figure.aria: Air passing up a spray chamber where recirculated water humidifies it from 35 to 25 degrees Celsius, with the water returning from the basin to the nozzles.

chapters.example: 1000 kg dry air/h enters an adiabatic spray chamber at 35 °C with Y = 0.010 and leaves at 25 °C. Find the outlet humidity and the water evaporated. Along the wet-bulb line the slope is about c_s/λ ≈ 0.00042 kg/kg per K, so dropping 35 → 25 °C raises Y by 0.0042, giving Y = 0.0142 ≈ 0.014. Water evaporated = 1000 × 0.0042 = 4.2 kg/h. Now cool the same outlet air to 15 °C: the saturation humidity at 15 °C is 0.0106, so 1000 × (0.014 − 0.0106) = 3.4 kg/h of water condenses.
chapters.trap: Expecting a cold water spray to dry the air; a spray can only humidify towards saturation, so dehumidification needs cooling below the dew point or a desiccant.
chapters.prereq: 7.1 to 7.3; Unit 3 for NTU and the enthalpy driving force in packed contactors.
chapters.leave: Water cooling by air to 7.5 and the drying of solids to 7.6 onwards.

chapters.idea: A cooling tower cools water by evaporating a small part of it into air, and the design rests on an enthalpy driving force integrated between the water inlet and outlet.
chapters.depth: Types: natural-draught atmospheric and hyperbolic towers, mechanical-draught forced and induced, counter-flow and cross-flow. Construction: fill or packing, water distribution nozzles, drift eliminators, louvers, fan, cold water basin. Define range (hot water minus cold water) and approach (cold water minus wet-bulb temperature) and show why the approach, not the dry bulb, sets the tower size. Write the heat balance L c_p dT = G dh and the Merkel equation KaV/L = ∫ dT/(h* − h) between the cold and hot water temperatures, with h* the saturation enthalpy at the water temperature and h the air enthalpy. Explain the tower characteristic, its dependence on L/G, NTU and HTU, and the four-point Chebyshev estimate of the integral. Cover evaporation loss, blowdown and cycles of concentration briefly, and fan power in one line.

figure.title: Counter-flow induced-draught tower, top to bottom
figure.aria: Vertical layers of a counter-flow cooling tower from the fan at the top through water distribution and fill to the cold water basin, with air rising against falling water.

chapters.example: A tower cools 1.0 kg/s of water from 40 °C to 30 °C. Air enters at a wet bulb of 24 °C and leaves at about 38 °C; dry air flow is 0.9 kg/s. Saturation enthalpies h* at 30, 35 and 40 °C are 99.7, 129.0 and 166.9 kJ/kg dry air. Find the heat load, the tower characteristic and the evaporation loss. Heat load = 1.0 × 4.187 × 10 = 41.9 kW. Inlet air (saturated at 24 °C): h₁ = 72.2, Y₁ = 0.0189. Air enthalpy rise = 41.9/0.9 = 46.5, so h₂ = 118.7 kJ/kg. Driving forces: bottom 99.7 − 72.2 = 27.5, middle 129.0 − 95.5 = 33.6, top 166.9 − 118.7 = 48.2. Simpson: KaV/L = (10/6)(1/27.5 + 4/33.6 + 1/48.2) = 0.29. Outlet Y = 0.031, so evaporation = 0.9 × (0.031 − 0.0189) = 0.011 kg/s ≈ 40 kg/h, about 1.1 % of the circulation.
chapters.trap: Using dry-bulb temperature for the approach, and using a temperature difference as the driving force in the Merkel integral instead of an enthalpy difference.
chapters.prereq: 7.3 for wet bulb and adiabatic saturation; Unit 2 for the heat and mass transfer coefficients behind the Merkel equation.
chapters.leave: Detailed fan and pump hydraulics to a mechanical engineering course; water treatment chemistry to a water treatment course.

chapters.idea: A wet solid holds water in different ways, and it stops drying when the solid's moisture equals the equilibrium moisture of the surrounding air.
chapters.depth: Define moisture content on a dry basis X (kg water per kg dry solid) and on a wet basis, with the conversion between them. Classify bound, unbound and free moisture, and define the equilibrium moisture content X* and the free moisture X − X*. Show the equilibrium isotherm of a hygroscopic solid against relative humidity, note the hysteresis between adsorption and desorption, and compare hygroscopic (wood, clay, food) with non-hygroscopic (sand, some salts) solids. Explain the drying mechanism: capillary flow, liquid and vapour diffusion inside the solid, evaporation at the surface, and the heat and mass transfer at the surface. Mention that the air temperature, humidity, velocity and the solid thickness set the rate, and preview the constant and falling rate periods.

figure.aria: An S-shaped equilibrium moisture isotherm rising steeply at high humidity, with the operating point at 40 percent relative humidity giving X-star equal to 0.10.

chapters.example: 100 kg of wet solid contains 30 kg of water. It is placed in air at 40 % relative humidity, for which the equilibrium moisture content is 0.10 kg/kg dry solid. Find the moisture on dry and wet bases, the free moisture and the mass of water that can be removed. Dry solid = 70 kg, so X = 30/70 = 0.429 kg/kg dry solid, and on a wet basis the moisture is 30/100 = 30 %. Free moisture = 0.429 − 0.10 = 0.329 kg/kg dry solid. Water removable = 0.329 × 70 = 23.0 kg, leaving 7.0 kg of water that this air can never take away.
chapters.trap: Assuming drying can go to zero moisture; every air humidity has a non-zero equilibrium moisture, and dry-basis and wet-basis moisture contents are easily swapped.
chapters.prereq: 7.1 for air humidity and 7.2 for relative humidity.
chapters.leave: The rate of drying to 7.7 and dryer hardware to 7.8.

chapters.idea: Plot the drying rate against moisture content, and the area under the reciprocal curve gives the drying time.
chapters.depth: Show how to get a rate curve from a batch test: weigh the sample with time, compute X, then R = −(m_s/A) dX/dt. Identify the constant-rate period, the critical moisture content X_c and the falling-rate period, with one linear falling-rate stage and a second diffusion-controlled stage for many solids. Derive the times: constant rate t = (m_s/(A R_c))(X₁ − X_c); falling rate to X* with a straight line through the origin t = (m_s X_c/(A R_c)) ln((X_c − X*)/(X₂ − X*)). Show the effect of air temperature, humidity and velocity (velocity matters only in the constant-rate period) and of thickness. Mention shrinkage and case hardening as reasons the real curve departs from the ideal one.

figure.aria: A drying rate curve that is flat at 1.5 from X equal to 0.40 down to the critical 0.20 and then falls in a curve towards zero at the equilibrium moisture.

chapters.example: 50 kg of dry solid with a drying area of 1 m² is dried from X₁ = 0.40 to X₂ = 0.10 kg/kg dry solid. The critical moisture is X_c = 0.20, the equilibrium moisture X* = 0.05 and the constant rate is R_c = 1.5 kg/(m²·h). Find the total drying time. Constant-rate period: t = (50/1.5)(0.40 − 0.20) = 6.67 h. Falling-rate period with a straight line to X*: t = (50 × 0.20/1.5) ln((0.20 − 0.05)/(0.10 − 0.05)) = 6.67 × 1.10 = 7.32 h. Total = 14.0 h.
chapters.trap: Using the constant-rate formula below X_c, and forgetting that R_c is per unit area of drying surface, not per kg of solid.
chapters.prereq: 7.6 for X, X* and the equilibrium moisture.
chapters.leave: Dryer types to 7.8 and full dryer sizing to 7.9.

chapters.idea: Dryers are chosen by how the solid behaves, and in through-circulation drying the air changes humidity as it climbs through the bed.
chapters.depth: Classify dryers into batch (tray or compartment, vacuum shelf, freeze) and continuous (tunnel, belt, rotary, drum, spray, fluidised bed, pneumatic or flash). For each give the feed form, the contact pattern and one typical use, such as spray drying of milk powder or tray drying of pottery. Treat through-circulation drying in detail: air pushed through a bed of granular solid, the pressure drop, and the rise of air humidity and fall of air temperature from the inlet face to the outlet face. Show the time calculation from an air humidity balance. Add dryer selection rules: heat sensitivity, particle size, tonnage, and the choice between direct and indirect heating.

figure.aria: A two-level tree splitting dryers into batch types such as tray, vacuum shelf and freeze, and continuous types such as tunnel, rotary, spray, fluidised bed and drum.

chapters.example: A through-circulation tray dryer handles 100 kg of dry solid, to be dried from X₁ = 0.25 to X₂ = 0.05 kg/kg dry solid. Air enters the bed at 60 °C with Y = 0.010 at 500 kg dry air/h and leaves at Y = 0.030. Find the drying time. Water to remove = 100 × (0.25 − 0.05) = 20 kg. Water picked up by the air = 500 × (0.030 − 0.010) = 10 kg/h. Drying time = 20/10 = 2.0 h. Check the air: it stays below saturation at the outlet temperature, so the bed is not rewetting the solid.
chapters.trap: Putting the tunnel dryer in the batch list, and confusing through-circulation (air passes through the bed) with cross-circulation (air passes over the tray surface).
chapters.prereq: 7.7 for drying rate and drying time.
chapters.leave: Detailed mechanical drawings to a machine design course and control loops to a process control course.

chapters.idea: A dryer design is a water balance, an air balance and a heat balance, followed by simple sizing rules that fix the diameter and length of the shell.
chapters.depth: Start from the water evaporated between the feed and product moisture. Get the dry air rate from the allowed humidity rise, then the volumetric flow from the humid volume at the outlet temperature. Size a rotary dryer: air mass velocity around 1.5 to 2.5 kg/(m²·s) fixes the diameter, and a length-to-diameter ratio of about 4 to 10 fixes the length; state the residence time and the shell slope and rotation. Describe the flights inside the shell that lift and shower the solids, and compare cocurrent with counter-current operation (cocurrent suits heat-sensitive solids). Add the heat duty and the drying efficiency as heat used for evaporation divided by heat supplied, allowing for heating the solids and the remaining moisture and for losses. Close with one line each on heat-pump, solar and waste-heat-recovery dryers as sustainable options.

figure.title: Sizing a rotary dryer
figure.aria: A five-step design chain from the water evaporated to the dry air rate, then the shell diameter, the shell length and the heat duty and efficiency.

chapters.example: A rotary dryer treats 1000 kg/h of wet solid at 25 % moisture (wet basis) and delivers it at 2 % moisture (wet basis). Air enters the heater at Y = 0.010 and leaves the dryer at Y = 0.035; the air mass velocity is 2.0 kg/(m²·s) and L/D = 6. Find the water evaporated, the air rate, the diameter and the length. Dry solid = 750 kg/h. Feed water = 250 kg/h; product water = 0.02/0.98 × 750 = 15.3 kg/h; evaporated = 234.7 ≈ 235 kg/h. Air rate = 235/(0.035 − 0.010) = 9400 kg dry air/h = 2.61 kg/s. Diameter: 2.61/2.0 = 1.31 m² of cross-section, so D = √(4 × 1.31/π) = 1.29 m, use 1.3 m. Length = 6 × 1.3 = 7.8 m, use 8 m.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the sensible heat needed to raise the solids and the remaining moisture to the outlet temperature, and confusing the dry air mass with the total humid air mass in the volumetric flow.
chapters.prereq: 7.1 for humid volume, 7.7 for drying time and 7.8 for dryer types.
chapters.leave: Detailed heat-exchanger and fan design to other courses; crystallisation and adsorption to Unit 6.
